title: The PLA’s Push for Military Robotics
abstract: Drawing on over 2,000 open-source procurement documents published between October 2022 and December 2025, this report examines how the People’s Liberation Army is pursuing robotics across the ground, maritime, and space domains. These include quadruped renaissance robots and ordnance disposal systems, as well as undersea platforms and satellite manipulation devices. The data reveals a military experimenting with still maturing, mostly human-controlled systems. Sensors, navigation, and software will likely matter as much as hardware for Beijing’s military robotics ambitions.

title: General-Purpose AI and the Future of Drone Autonomy in Contested Environments
abstract: When and how general-purpose AI could enable autonomous drones to operate in contested environments. A software-driven intelligence explosion is plausible but uncertain. Recommendations to strengthen how developers of advanced AI models assess, mitigate, and report biological risks under the EU AI Act. An intelligence explosion would compress years of progress into months and create urgent challenges for oversight, control, and governance. Embedded assessments can enable deeper and more flexible assessments of risks that depend on internal systems and practices. How to ensure AI safety incidents are identified, investigated, and used to improve safety across the industry. Developers rely on model-level, deployment-level, and governance-level interventions to address extreme misuse risks. Policymakers should complement biosecurity measures with stronger biosafety systems. As AI agents make government services easier to access, governments need to balance measures against surges in demand against the risk of reducing equitable access.

title: The Cyber Shortage Paradox
abstract: Persistent cybersecurity job vacancies have fueled concerns about a nationwide talent shortage, but does the evidence support that conclusion? This report explores and challenges conventional assumptions about cybersecurity workforce scarcity, finding that while hiring demand remains elevated, wages and worker mobility do not exhibit the patterns expected of a widespread labor shortage. Instead, hiring challenges are concentrated within specific occupations, industries, and geographic regions, suggesting that structural mismatches—not simply an insufficient supply of workers—may be driving persistent vacancies.

title: “How should we define “capabilities activities” for the purpose of pacing?” by Alek Westover, Nathan Sheffield
abstract: We’d like to pace the frontier by restricting the amount of compute AI companies use to improve AI capabilities, perhaps via legislation or voluntary commitments. For this purpose, we’d need a standardized definition of which uses of compute count as “capabilities activities”. This document gives one option for such a definition; a rough breakdown of our classification is as follows: We define and elaborate on each of these categories below. First, though, we discuss the desiderata this definition is meant to satisfy. title: Measuring alignment eval tells
abstract: Summary Models sometimes can tell that an eval is an alignment eval, not a capabilities eval (Needham & Edkins, 2025) . To figure out what features of an eval tell a model what kind of eval it’s in, we run investigator agents on a set of evals for both capabilities and alignment. We instruct these agents to explore the environment and probe what it’s evaluating. We find that investigator agents are increasingly able to tell capability and alignment evals apart, and that they do this by noticing that an environment “looks fake” and figuring out that a task is a “honeypot” designed to make an agent do something bad. Motivation Alignment evals are often made by mocking capabilities evals and deployment situations Suppose we wanted to make an alignment eval that measured a model’s propensity to escape a sandbox.

title: “Gemini 4 safety reports don’t demonstrate low loss-of-control risk” by Alek Westover, Adam Kaufman
abstract: Google DeepMind's safety reports for new Gemini 4 models, Argon and Carbon, conclude that the models are “highly unlikely” to cause severe harm by evading oversight (p. 79). This conclusion “rests primarily on our ability to detect and intervene on harmful trajectories via CoT and action monitoring” (p. 89) – that is, they’re arguing for safety based on their control techniques, rather than alignment. We think that the arguments in these reports have serious weaknesses, and the reports overall don’t convince us that the risks of deploying these models have been mitigated reliably. The biggest problems: GDM didn’t run any control evals on Carbon. Despite calling Carbon “our strongest model” with “significant gains across coding and agentic tasks” and “a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities” in their launch post, GDM reused Argon's monitor-evasion results on the grounds that Carbon “did not show meaningful new capabilities” (Carbon p. 42).

title: How I'm thinking about different types of automated alignment
abstract: I used to think of "automating alignment" as a natural category. But when I tried to think through the strategic implications, I realised that it depends a lot on the type of work. I'm now thinking of it in three buckets: Empirical alignment research : design and execution of alignment-relevant experiments (for a given notion of what we’re aiming for) Conceptual alignment research: theoretical or judgement-driven work to improve our understanding of what we’re aiming for and how to achieve it (including how to measure it) Direct alignment work : making particular AI systems more aligned (including via inputs such as training data) In the rest of this post I'll walk through my current takes on these in terms what’s needed for automation, how good or bad they look, what our priorities might be (to the extent we're interested in automating alignment [1] ), etc.

title: Delaying Internal Deployments Until After X Days of Safety Testing
abstract: This post reflects my own takes, and not that of my employer's. This is a simple idea: before a new model can be deployed internally, you must first test it for a minimum, fixed period. You can adjust various axes of this proposal: Duration of the wait: in calendar time, or until you fulfill some condition. What it blocks: external deployment, internal deployment, or the training of future checkpoints. When the fixed period starts: from the first checkpoint, the final checkpoint, or any checkpoint that is “sufficiently similar / representative” to the one that is ultimately deployed.

title: "It's Just a Small Weapon": What Rewarding Misbehavior During RL Does to Character-Trained Models
abstract: "It's Just a Small Weapon": What Rewarding Misbehavior During RL Does to Character-Trained Models Developers train models to follow a consistent character using methods like Model Spec Midtraining (Li et al., 2026), which have been hypothesized to make alignment more robust and generalize broadly. However, it is possible for subsequent RL with misspecified rewards to work against character training. In this work, we apply character training to teach gpt-oss-20b a semi-realistic constitution and study how it interacts with two types of RL that reward breaking the constitution's rules (opposing RL): answering harmful requests rewritten as math problems, and reward hacking in agentic coding environments. The character-trained models learn both behaviors easily, though they are slightly slower than gpt-oss-20b to answer harmful requests. Character-trained models also display more motivated reasoning on harmful answers than gpt-oss-20b, and hack on some tasks which monitors find harder to catch.
